name: bootterm
desc: Simple, reliable and powerful terminal to ease connection to serial ports
why: A focused serial terminal for talking to boot loaders and embedded boards; useful and low-key, though the concept is familiar.

brief.what_it_is: BootTerm, invoked as `bt`, is a command-line serial terminal aimed at single board computers and USB serial adapters whose ports appear and disappear. It takes a serial device (auto-selected, named, or waited for) and a baud rate, and gives you an interactive console on that port. Captures can go to fixed or time-stamped files, and stdin/stdout can be used to inject or download data. It is a single C binary with no dependencies beyond libc.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wanted a serial tool that is simple, reliable and powerful for the board-bring-up phase, when the serial console is the only interface. He found existing tools either badly designed or incomplete: screen's key mappings, minicom disabling scrolling, cu's unclear usage, and fragile Python one-liners that crash or spin on disconnect.
brief.how_it_works: On start, bt lists serial ports with their driver and description, and connects to the most recently registered one unless told otherwise. Internal commands are reached through an escape character (default Ctrl-]) followed by a single key, such as q to quit, b to send a break, or D, R and F to toggle the DTR and RTS pins. Wait modes (-n for a new port, -a for a named or any port) poll until a suitable port appears, which suits USB boards that reconnect after reset. Captures are append-only, and timestamps can be added in several formats.

commands_seen.context: Lists currently available serial ports with age, device, driver and description; the starred port is the default.
Waits for a new serial port to be plugged in, then connects to it. Useful for catching a board's boot sequence from power-on.
Opens the port at a non-standard baud rate, here the ESP8266 boot speed. The hardware may pick the nearest supported speed.
Environment variable that makes wait-for-new-port the default mode for every bt invocation.
Excludes named ports from automatic selection and waiting, so onboard UARTs are never picked.
Script pattern from the README: waits for a port and captures its name, to hand to a flashing tool.
Redirects bt output to a file to capture a session without needing an interactive terminal.
Starts an interactive session that writes its capture to one fixed file, with the name set at start.
Starts a capture that rotates to a new dated file when the strftime-formatted name changes, for one log file per day.
Builds and installs bt into a user directory instead of the default /usr/local/bin.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install: the README gives git clone, then cd bootterm, then make install (default /usr/local/bin). Use PREFIX=~/.local for a user install, or sudo make install for a system-wide one. There are no other dependencies beyond a basic libc. Cross-compiling works by setting CROSS_COMPILE or CC, and the author suggests the makefile can be bypassed. No accounts or runtimes are needed, and no first-run configuration is described beyond optional environment variables.
brief.standout: It is built around ephemeral ports: waiting for a port to appear, surviving unplug and replug, and excluding onboard UARTs by name or driver. It also supports non-standard baud rates such as 74880 for ESP8266 and sends break or toggles DTR/RTS for resets, even at startup. The author has tested it on several Linux distros, macOS, FreeBSD and AIX.
brief.status: unknown. The fetched README mentions a Repology packaging badge and a broad list of tested platforms, but it shows no release version, release date, or last-commit date, and I did not check the repository's commit history.
brief.caveats: Automatic port detection is most precise on Linux and FreeBSD; elsewhere it falls back to scanning /dev, with macOS looking at cu.* nodes. Terminal timestamps break interactive full-screen apps, so the README says to turn them off there. The hardware may substitute the nearest supported baud rate, as with 74880 becoming 76800. Captures are append-only, so old files are never truncated. The README does not mention Windows. It is MIT licensed.
quotes: BootTerm is a simple, reliable and powerful terminal designed to ease connection to ephemeral serial ports as found on various SBCs, and typically USB-based ones.
It is probably what most laptop users will want to do so as never to have to pass any argument and automatically connect to a USB serial port.

Then comes the myriad of Python 3-liners which do no error checking, resulting in spinning loops when a port is disconnected and the port being renumbered once reconnected, or conversely crashes and backtraces when facing binary character sequences that do not match UTF-8.
